cards.title: What the mind rests on
cards.body: Today's pieces share a quiet question: what does the mind stand on? You will find it in the body's immune system, in the fear left by East Germany's state watching its own people, still felt decades later, and even in what physicists mean by 'reality'. If you read one thing, read the psychosis case study. For a few people, their hallucinations came from their own immune system attacking the brain, and immune treatment can bring them fully back.

cards.title: Consciousness science is stuck. Is the 'stream' to blame?
cards.body: Since 1990, neuroscientists have searched for the exact brain activity behind each conscious experience. Progress has stalled. One essay says the tools are not the problem. The problem is a common-sense belief hidden inside the search: that consciousness flows as one continuous stream.

sections.text:
A word flashes on a screen. A moment ago you had not noticed it. Now you have. Something in your brain changed at that instant. For decades, neuroscientists have built experiments to catch exactly that change.

This was the old hope. In 1990, Christof Koch and Francis Crick gave it a name: the search for the "neural correlates of consciousness," or NCC. A neural correlate is brain activity that goes along with something. Here it means the smallest set of brain processes that is enough to produce one specific experience. The idea was that if you found that set, you would find where experience happens.

The plan had a real strength. It tried to be "theory-neutral." That meant collecting data first, without betting on any one big theory of what consciousness is. You just watch the brain and note what lines up with experience.

Today the mood is different. The tools are better and the data keep growing. Yet even top scientists admit that progress has fallen short of early hopes. People disagree about why. Some blame the definitions, because the word "consciousness" keeps changing meaning. Some blame the tools, because brain measures are still rough, especially in humans. Others point to something deeper. Science looks from the outside, in the third person. Experience is known only from the inside, in the first person.

The authors of this essay give a different answer. The problem, they say, is a belief so ordinary that we rarely notice it: that waking life is one continuous stream of consciousness. In this picture, the stream flows all day. Perceptions, memories and thoughts step into it and drop out of it, moment by moment.

That picture quietly shaped the NCC search. If experience is a stream, then at every moment some brain events must match whatever is in the stream right now. So experiments look for the instant when something seen, a memory or an idea "enters consciousness," like the flashing word. Then they look for the brain change that comes with it.

This is the turning point. The NCC approach was meant to take no side on theory. But by assuming a stream, the authors argue, it took a side without saying so. A theory slipped in without anyone noticing. They suggest this hidden assumption may be what led the field to a dead end.

Put the two views side by side. The old view said the hard part was measurement: find the right brain signal at the right moment. The new view says the question itself may be wrong. If experience does not flow as a smooth stream, there may be no "moment of entering" to find. Asking what the brain does at that moment may mean asking about something that does not exist in that form.

Doubting the stream is only a first step, not an answer. If experience is not a stream, what shape does it have? Until that is clear, scientists do not know exactly what brain activity they are looking for.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The authors do not attack the goal of the NCC approach. They call it admirable: gather evidence before betting on a theory. Their complaint is about how the goal was carried out. Something that looked like plain common sense was really a theory.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Sometimes a search fails not because the answer is hidden, but because the question carries a hidden picture.

recall.q: What hidden assumption do the authors say got into the search for the neural correlates of consciousness, and why is it a problem?
recall.a: The assumption is that consciousness is one continuous stream, so at every moment some brain activity must match what is in it. The NCC search was meant to be theory-neutral, but this assumption is itself a theory. The authors think it may be why the field is stuck.

cards.title: RBI sells ₹1 trillion in bonds to pull cash out of banks
cards.body: This financial year, the RBI has sold ₹1 trillion (₹1 lakh crore) more in government bonds than it bought. That is its biggest net sale in more than a decade. Selling bonds takes cash out of the banking system. Banks pay the RBI for the bonds, and that money leaves the system.

sections.label: Why now
sections.text: The RBI let banks raise US dollars through a special window. This added to India's forex reserves and helped the rupee while oil prices rose. But it also left banks with too much cash. So the overnight rate fell below the RBI's policy rate. The overnight rate is what banks charge each other for one-day loans. Taking cash out pushes that rate back up.

sections.label: The numbers
items: ₹900 billion: the last record, in FY2018, during demonetisation
₹2 trillion: where traders expect total sales to be by December
₹1–1.5 trillion: more sales one treasury head expects in October and November

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: This fits a tighter money policy. Most people in a Reuters poll expect the RBI to raise its policy rate next week. The government has also cut how many 3-year and 5-year bonds it will issue for the rest of the year. Traders say this gives the RBI room to sell more.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: ICBC's treasury head expects one of two things: another ₹1 trillion in bond sales, or a higher cash reserve ratio. That ratio is the share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI. Either way, more cash leaves the system.

recall.q: Why is the RBI selling so many bonds this year, and how does selling bonds help?
recall.a: A special window for raising dollars helped the rupee, but it left banks with too much cash. That pushed the overnight rate below the RBI's policy rate. When banks buy bonds, they pay the RBI in cash, and that cash leaves the system. This pushes short-term rates back up.

cards.title: When psychosis is the immune system attacking the brain
cards.body: In a few people, hallucinations and paranoia come from the immune system attacking the brain. For them, immune treatment can bring a full recovery where psychiatric drugs failed. But these cases are rare. Most experts say they are 1 to 2 percent of psychosis at most.
cards.evidence: case reports + early screening (~5,000 patients) · trial of 70 patients, results due 2027

sections.text:
On a psychiatric ward in Cambridge, England, a man reached out and stroked an animal that was not there. He talked with these creatures "in as real a way as he was with me," says Peter Jones, the psychiatrist treating him.

Antipsychotic drugs, the usual medicine for psychosis, did nothing. Then the team tried plasma exchange. This treatment filters the blood to remove antibodies. Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to fight invaders. The animals faded away.

The man did not have schizophrenia. He had autoimmune encephalitis. This is swelling in the brain, caused by the body's own defenses attacking it. His case was also hard to spot. Most patients show clear nerve signs, such as seizures. He showed none. If Jones had not suspected the immune system, the case would likely have been missed.

How can antibodies cause hallucinations? A key paper in 2007 described 12 women with this illness. Nine of them first showed psychosis-like symptoms. Their antibodies stuck to NMDA receptors. These are proteins on brain cells that help with learning and memory. The trigger was a tumor, most often in the ovaries. The tumors held nerve tissue with the same receptors. So the immune system learned to treat the receptor as an enemy. Then it attacked the same receptor in the healthy brain. Swelling followed, and with it, psychosis.

The good news: this can be treated. Doctors test the blood or spinal fluid for the antibodies. They remove any tumor and give drugs that calm the immune system. Many patients recover fully. Belinda Lennox, an Oxford psychiatrist, saw a young librarian who became paranoid, stopped sleeping, and then went silent. Antipsychotics made her worse. After the antibodies were removed from her blood, she was completely better in about a week.

Now the honest numbers. About 3 percent of people have a psychotic episode in their lifetime. Most experts say autoimmune causes explain 1 to 2 percent of those cases at most. Nearly everyone with psychosis needs standard psychiatric care.

The open question is whether more quiet cases, like the man with the animals, are hiding. Lennox and Jones run a trial called SINAPPS2. They tested about 5,000 people with recent psychosis and no serious nerve signs. Around 5 percent had the antibodies. But a positive test is not proof. Some results are false alarms. Some people carry antibodies that do no harm. So 70 patients are getting either immune treatment or a placebo, a dummy treatment. Results are expected in 2027.

The opposite danger is real too. A 2022 study across six specialist clinics found that just over a quarter of people diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis did not have it. The treatment has risks. It weakens the body's defense against infection, and steroids can make psychosis worse. In that study, 84 patients got immune treatment, and 20 percent of them had a bad reaction. Their real illness went untreated, or was treated late.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Much of the hope rests on single dramatic cases. Jones also remembers patients who looked similar but did not have an autoimmune illness. The trial that should settle the question has not reported yet. Until it does, as Jones says, the question stays open.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: For a rare few, psychosis is a fight inside the body, and it can be won. The mistake is to forget how rare they are.

recall.q: How can the immune system cause psychosis, and how common is this among all psychosis cases?
recall.a: In autoimmune encephalitis, antibodies attack proteins on brain cells, such as NMDA receptors. The brain swells, and this can bring hallucinations and paranoia. Immune treatment can fully cure some patients. But most experts say it explains 1 to 2 percent of psychosis at most, so nearly everyone with psychosis still needs standard psychiatric care.

cards.title: Stuck in your own head? Russell's advice: look outward
cards.body: Bertrand Russell warned that if all your happiness depends on your own life, you will ask for more than life can give, and you will get less. His fix: widen your interests and meet the world in a friendly way. You come back to your worries calmer and better able to handle them.

sections.text:
Some nights your mind walks the same small circle. The worry about work. The conversation you keep replaying. The question of what is wrong with you. You try to think your way out, and it does not work. That is not a failure on your part. The circle itself is the problem.

Maria Popova, who writes The Marginalian, says one thing has saved her in her darkest hours, again and again. She calls it unselfing: waking up to some part of the world that is not you. A hand held out to someone else who is struggling. A galaxy just discovered, millions of light-years away. A cardinal (a small red bird) shaking a little in the tree outside her window. For a moment, your own self stops filling the whole room.

In 1930, Bertrand Russell, the Nobel-winning philosopher and mathematician, gave this idea its reasoning in his book The Conquest of Happiness. The world is huge, and your powers are small. If all your happiness depends on your own situation, you will ask life for more than it can give. And asking too much, he writes, is "the surest way of getting even less" than you could have had.

So he suggests a trade. Find a real interest in something outside yourself. His examples are almost funny in how far away they are: the Council of Trent, a church meeting from the 1500s, or the life story of stars. If you can forget your worries in a subject like that, you gain two things. While you are away, you feel real happiness, even if it does not last. And when you come back to your problems, you bring a calm and balance that help you deal with them in the best way.

Notice what he does not say. He does not say your worries are fake, or that you should ignore them. He says you will face them better after a trip away. The trip is not running away. It is how you get your strength back.

Then comes his rule, an idea he would expand in his final years. Let your interests be as wide as possible. And let your reactions to the things and people that interest you be, as far as possible, "friendly rather than hostile." Wide, and warm.

Popova draws out the lesson: happiness is less something you chase and more something you give in to. The wonder of the world, as it comes.

So pick one thing that is not you. A friend's problem you can help with. A question about the stars. The bird outside. Give it your full, friendly attention, and let your own story wait at the door. It will still be there when you come back. You will meet it steadier than you left it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: You rarely think your way out of your own head. You get interested in something else, and you walk out.

recall.q: According to Russell, what goes wrong when all our happiness depends on our own situation, and what does he recommend instead?
recall.a: We ask more of life than it can give, and asking too much gets us even less. Instead, make your interests as wide as possible and your reactions to things and people friendly rather than hostile. Time spent lost in the wider world gives real happiness and brings back the calm to handle your worries well.

cards.title: How your brain speaks and listens in one conversation
cards.body: A small brain-scan study suggests that speaking and listening share the same brain code for the last few seconds of talk. Over longer stretches, they split apart. Speaking stays focused on what was just said. Listening holds on to the bigger picture.
cards.evidence: single study · n=8 · fMRI brain scans

sections.text:
When you talk with someone, you often start planning your reply while they are still speaking. So your brain does two jobs at almost the same time. It builds the words you want to say. It also makes sense of the words coming in. In real talk, you switch between these jobs every few seconds.

How does one brain manage both? The simple picture of turn-taking, where you listen and then you speak, does not explain it. The two jobs overlap too much. So the real question is this: does the brain use one shared code for meaning, whether you speak or listen? Or does it keep the two jobs apart?

Both simple answers have problems. If it is one shared pool, how do you keep track of who said what, and who knows what? If there are two separate systems, the brain would have to translate between them at every turn. Older research could not settle this. Most of it had people listen to single sentences or read long stories alone. Nobody was talking back.

A team led by Masahiro Yamashita and Shinji Nishimoto in Japan tried something closer to real life. Eight native Japanese speakers lay in an fMRI scanner. This is a machine that tracks blood flow as a sign of brain activity. Using a microphone and earphones, each person chatted freely with a researcher for about three hours. They talked about everyday things, like their favorite classes.

Real speech is messy. So the team gave the written record of each talk to a GPT-style AI language model. The model turned the words into number patterns that capture meaning. The team did this for stretches of talk from 1 to 32 seconds long. Then they checked which patterns best predicted each person's brain activity.

The answer depended on the length of the stretch. For short stretches of 1 to 4 seconds, speaking and listening used the same code. It showed up in overlapping areas across the front, sides and top of the brain. For long stretches of 16 to 32 seconds, the shared code broke apart. It was spread across the brain and looked different in each person. Sometimes it reached areas linked to guessing what others think and to recalling memories. So the quick work looked the same in everyone, but each person tracked the bigger picture in their own way.

The two jobs also preferred opposite time spans. Brain areas used only for speaking worked mostly with short context. That makes sense, because you must react fast to what was just said. Areas used only for listening worked with long context, across several sentences. You need that to build a full picture of what the other person means.

Some areas handled both jobs, but with separate patterns. This only happened once eight seconds or more of context was counted. The authors think these areas help keep your point of view apart from your partner's.

One small surprise: fillers like "yeah" and "uh" had their own brain patterns. They take almost no effort to say, but they keep the talk flowing. The brain seems to handle them apart from statements of fact.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Only eight people took part, and all were native Japanese speakers. That is a very small group. The team also skipped the usual first scans that map known brain networks, such as the one for reading other minds. So they cannot say exactly which networks their results belong to. Larger studies with better brain maps are needed.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: In the moment, speaker and listener share one code. What each person takes from the whole conversation is their own.

recall.q: How did the length of a stretch of talk change whether speaking and listening shared a brain code?
recall.a: For short stretches of 1 to 4 seconds, speaking and listening used the same code in overlapping brain areas. For long stretches of 16 to 32 seconds, the shared code broke apart and looked different in each person. Speaking also leaned on short context, while listening leaned on long context.

cards.title: Islam and love: the word that put a Sufi on trial
cards.body: In 878, a Sufi in Baghdad was put on trial for his life for saying he loved God. The love was not the problem. The word was: ishq, the poets' word for obsessive, bodily passion. The Qur'an never uses it. Later Sufis chose it on purpose.

sections.text:
Baghdad, the year 878. A Sufi (a Muslim mystic) named Abu l-Husayn al-Nuri is on trial for his life. One charge: people heard him say, "I passionately love God, and He passionately loves me."

The prosecutor did not object to the love. Every Muslim was supposed to love God. He objected to the word. Nuri used the verb ashiqa, from ishq: the word for a man's love for a woman. Obsessive, bodily, unreasonable. Using it for God, the prosecutor said, was indecent and close to unbelief. Nuri was set free. But the argument went on for four more centuries. It produced one of the richest bodies of writing about love in any religion. Here is what it teaches.

1. The question was never whether to love God, only how. Love was never a side topic in Islam. At the trial, no one doubted that loving God was right. The danger was in the kind of love, and the word for it.

2. Islam spoke about love in many voices, and they did not agree. The Qur'an (Islam's holy book) speaks of love in dozens of places. Islamic law governs marriage and family ties. One school of theology (reasoned thinking about God) relied on logic. It was nervous about saying God feels emotions at all. The philosophers were deeply shaped by Plato and Aristotle. The Sufis made love the answer to every question, and they went deepest.

3. The Qur'an's own word for love is plain, and it runs both ways. That word is hubb, with a close twin, mahabba. Its root also gives the Arabic word for a seed. It covers affection, attachment, preference and devotion. God's love for people is hubb. People's love for God is hubb too. The word is morally neutral: you can have hubb for money or for God. Arabic also has wudd, or mawadda: warm, steady affection.

4. The most dangerous word was the one the mystics wanted. Ishq is passionate, excessive love, love that has become a kind of sickness. Its root may be linked to the word for a creeping vine that strangles the tree it holds. It belonged to the love poets, not the Qur'an. The Sufis took it anyway, and for exactly that reason. The prosecutor feared a love that could not be controlled. That was the love the Sufis wanted to name.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The fight was never about whether to love God. It was about whether that love should be allowed to overwhelm you.

recall.q: Why was Nuri put on trial over his love for God, and why did the Sufis want his word anyway?
recall.a: Loving God was not the problem, since every Muslim was supposed to. The problem was the word, ishq: the word for obsessive, bodily love between a man and a woman, which the Qur'an never uses. The Sufis chose it because it named a love that overwhelms the lover and cannot be controlled, unlike the Qur'an's plain, neutral word, hubb.

cards.title: AI chatbots are more hopeful about AI's future than people are
cards.body: Guess first: who feels better about AI's future, AI chatbots or ordinary people? Researchers gave seven chatbots and 337 people the same 39-question survey about AGI (artificial general intelligence). AGI means a future AI that could do any mental task a human can. Each answer was scored from 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive).
cards.evidence: single study · 7 AI models vs 337 people, mostly from Serbia · 1–5 rating survey

sections.text:
You might guess the chatbots would sound worried. They learn from internet text, and much of it shows AI as a threat. The opposite happened. Every chatbot scored above the human average.

The lead author thinks fine-tuning may explain it. Fine-tuning is the later stage where companies shape how a model answers. But he admits no one knows for sure.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Chatbots' average: 3.77. People's average: 2.97.
Most hopeful: GPT-4 at 4.12. Its maker's stated goal is to build AGI.
Least hopeful: Google's Bard at 3.32. That is still above the people.
The people came from three online groups, mostly in Serbia.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Millions of people ask chatbots about AI every day. A small tilt, repeated that often, could quietly change what everyone thinks is normal. But this is one study with a small, mostly Serbian sample. It is a first look, not a final answer.

recall.q: How did the chatbots' views on AI's future compare with people's, and why could that matter?
recall.a: Every chatbot was more hopeful than the people: 3.77 on average versus 2.97 out of 5, with GPT-4 highest at 4.12. So many people ask chatbots about AI that even a small tilt could slowly shift public opinion. It is one small study, though, and most of the people were from Serbia.

cards.title: Psychedelics change how signals reach the brain's 'self' network
cards.body: LSD, psilocybin and MDMA seem to cut the flow of fresh sensory signals into the brain network behind daydreaming and self-talk. The pattern showed up in people and in mice. But in one small group, the people with the biggest drop felt the most out of control, not the most at peace.
cards.evidence: four small datasets · n=14 (MDMA), 6 (psilocybin), 18 (LSD) humans + 14 mice · healthy volunteers only · brain imaging

sections.text:
A rain gauge in one town tells you how much rain fell. It cannot tell you where the storm came from or where it is going. For that, you need a weather radar.

Most brain scans have worked like rain gauges. They measure activity in fixed spots. A Stanford team led by Adam Pines and Leanne Williams wanted the radar view. They borrowed a video method called optical flow, which tracks how pixels move from frame to frame. They used it to follow waves of activity moving across the cortex, the brain's outer layer.

They watched the default mode network. This is a set of brain regions that gets busy when you turn inward: daydreaming, thinking about yourself, replaying the past. It is also linked to rigid thinking, and it does not work normally in many mental illnesses. It sits at the top of the brain's processing ladder. Signals flow up into it from the senses (bottom-up), bringing fresh news from the world. Signals also flow down from it (top-down), bringing expectations built from past experience. A healthy mind needs both.

What we know. The same pattern showed up across four small datasets. In 14 people on MDMA, 18 on LSD and 6 on psilocybin, the waves moving through this network got weaker. With MDMA and LSD, a smaller share of signals also travelled bottom-up into the network. Psilocybin pointed the same way, but that result could have been chance. The team thinks the drug's effects lasted for days and blurred the comparison scans. In 14 mice, a method that records brain cells directly found the same drop with LSD. So the effect seems to be real nerve activity, not a side effect of how scanners measure blood flow. The anti-anxiety drug diazepam cut bottom-up flow a little. The sedative dexmedetomidine raised it.

What we don't know. Everyone studied was healthy. So nobody can yet say whether this change explains why psychedelics may help depression. One idea is that less bottom-up flow quiets rumination: the automatic, looping thoughts found in some depression. That is a guess, not a finding. The same logic raises a worry. People at risk of psychosis already have trouble with bottom-up signals. Cutting those signals further might make them worse.

What's contested. The popular story says psychedelics heal by quieting the ego. This study makes that story less simple. In the MDMA group, people with the biggest drop in bottom-up flow felt the least in control. They also felt more fear of losing their sense of self, which researchers call 'ego dissolution'. Bottom-up signals seem to keep us anchored in the world around us. Cut them too far, and a quieter self may feel less like peace and more like drifting.

How we would find out: bigger samples, real patients instead of healthy volunteers, and checking whether this brain change predicts who actually gets better.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: All four samples are small, so they cannot show how much people differ in their reactions. The method only tracks the brain's surface, not the deep parts that psychedelics also affect. Human scanners also miss very fast changes.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Quieting the voice inside only helps if the world outside can still get in.

recall.q: What did the psychedelics do to signals entering the default mode network, and why does the MDMA result make the 'quiet the ego' story less simple?
recall.a: They weakened the waves moving through the network and cut the share of bottom-up signals coming in from the senses. But in the MDMA group, people with the biggest drop felt the least in control and feared losing their sense of self more. Losing that link to the outside world may feel frightening, not healing.

cards.title: Becoming a father is a creative act, not only biology
cards.body: Coleridge met his newborn son with stiff poems and distance. Then he stayed home, warmed diapers on his knee, and wrote his greatest work. An Aeon essay argues that a father is made by time and care, not given at the birth.

sections.text:
In February 1797, Samuel Taylor Coleridge sat in a small cottage in Somerset, England. A cloth diaper was pinned on his knee to warm for his baby son. His eyes were on the ceiling, hunting for a line of poetry. He described the scene in a letter to a friend.

Five months earlier, he was a different man. When his son Hartley was born, Coleridge was far away, preaching in Birmingham. He answered the news with three cool, careful sonnets. A few days later he told a friend he had seen better-looking babies. Then he moved his family to the cottage and took on the house jobs himself: cook, cleaner, part-time nurse. Within 18 months of the birth, he had begun or finished “Kubla Khan”, “Christabel” and “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner”. These are the poems that made his name.

The English scholar Daniel Swift builds an essay around this change. Its core is two short passages:

“The creation of the father is also the creation of the poet.”

“The process of becoming a father – quite literally, thinking your way into it – is itself a creative act, driven by time, proximity and a sense of responsibility.”

Let's read them piece by piece.

“The creation of the father.” The key word is creation. A man does not fully become a father on the day of the birth. In September, Coleridge was a father on paper but not in feeling. The father was made later, in the cottage, through daily work.

“Also the creation of the poet.” This goes against an old story. In the Iliad, the hero Hector lifts his baby son, hands him back, and returns to war. In 1938 the critic Cyril Connolly called the pram in the hall, meaning a baby at home, the enemy of good art. Swift says the opposite: the months that made the father also made the artist. Robert Lowell is another case. His daughter Harriet was born in January 1957. By the end of that year, at 40, Lowell had written his first poems without a fixed rhythm. His next book, Life Studies, started “confessional” poetry, which is poetry about private family life.

“Thinking your way into it.” Swift means this literally. Brain scans show that new fathers' brains change. The cortex, the brain's outer layer, loses some volume. The links between brain regions change too. In one study, fathers who felt more purpose after the birth had more connections in two places. One was the temporal poles, part of the mentalising network. This is the system we use to imagine what others think and feel. The other was the hippocampus, a memory center. The psychologist Darby Saxbe reads this as the brain helping new fathers feel that fatherhood means something.

“Time, proximity and a sense of responsibility.” Proximity means closeness. Notice what is missing from this list: genes. A 2014 study in Israel scanned gay male couples raising babies who were adopted or born through surrogacy. The father who did most of the daily care showed activity in the amygdala, an emotion center, like mothers who were main caregivers. He also showed the mentalising activity seen in other fathers, with a stronger link between the two. Care, not blood, shaped this father's brain.

So fatherhood is not only a fact of biology. A parent is made the way a poem is made: by staying close, giving hours, and carrying the weight. The same may be true of anything we inherit, like a family, a role or a name. It is handed to us, but it only becomes ours through the work we put in. Far away, Coleridge wrote careful, distant verse. With a diaper on his knee, he wrote his best work.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Swift admits the limits. Brain scientists show links, not causes, so tying brain changes to a new style of poetry is a guess. Coleridge's breakthrough also owed a lot to his friendship with Wordsworth. And a pattern is not a rule: it happens often, not always.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody is handed parenthood at the birth. You make it by staying close.

recall.q: According to the essay, what actually makes someone a father, and what evidence suggests genes are not the key ingredient?
recall.a: Becoming a father is a creative act. It is built over time through closeness, daily care and responsibility, not all at once at the birth. A 2014 study of gay fathers raising adopted or surrogate-born babies found that the main caregiver's brain changed like a caring parent's. So care, not genes, shaped it.

cards.title: US spares India from 100% tariff on some specialty drugs
cards.body: India and 19 other countries will reportedly be exempt from a new 100% US tariff on some patented drugs. Drugs for rare diseases and infertility, and the ingredients used to make them, will face no tariff.

sections.text:
The news comes from a report in The Economic Times. It is not a final official list.

A tariff is a tax on imported goods. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation (a formal order) that put a 100% tariff on certain patented medicines. These are drugs that only the patent owner may make for a set time. At 100%, the tax equals the drug's full import value.

For Indian companies that ship these drugs to the US, the exemption removes that 100% tax.

One detail is unclear. The report also mentions 20 places with US trade agreements, so the exact number of countries may differ.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 0%: the tariff on exempted rare-disease and infertility drugs, and their ingredients
20: India plus 19 other countries covered, per the report
28 September 2026: date of the report

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Watch for the official US list. It should confirm which countries and drugs qualify, and whether the count is 19 or 20. Until then, treat this as likely, not final.

recall.q: Which drugs from India escape the new 100% US tariff, and why is this not yet final?
recall.a: Drugs for rare diseases and infertility, and the ingredients used to make them. The news comes from a media report, not a final official list, and even the report's country count is unclear.

cards.title: SpaceX's Starship tries to reach orbit for the first time
cards.body: Starship, the biggest rocket ever built, has flown 13 times since April 2023. It has never reached orbit. Flight 14, set for Monday, September 28, is its first try.

sections.text:
All 13 earlier flights were suborbital. The rocket went up and came back down without circling Earth. The longest flight lasted 65 minutes.

Starship has two parts. The lower stage, Super Heavy, should splash down in the Gulf of Mexico about seven minutes after liftoff, as on earlier flights. The upper stage, called Ship, aims for low Earth orbit. There it should release 26 new Starlink Version 3 internet satellites and circle Earth six times. Then it should splash down in the Pacific off Chile, about 10 hours after launch. The launch is from Starbase in South Texas, with a 75-minute window.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Both stages are built to be fully and quickly reused. SpaceX calls this the "holy grail of rocketry." NASA has already picked Ship as the first crewed lander for its Artemis moon program, which aims to land people on the moon in 2028.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 407 feet (124 m): Starship's full height. Ship alone is 171 feet (52 m).
100,000: satellites Musk says the new Starlink network will reach. About 11,000 Starlinks fly today. The 26 on board are the first.
3: times SpaceX has caught Super Heavy with the tower's "chopstick" arms. It has never tried this with Ship.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Even a perfect flight leaves big steps undone. SpaceX must still catch Ship at the tower. It must show it can move fuel from one ship to another in orbit, which deep-space trips will need. And Ship needs a life-support system before it can carry people.

recall.q: What makes Flight 14 different from Starship's first 13 flights, and what is Ship supposed to do on it?
recall.a: All 13 earlier flights were suborbital. They went up and came down without circling Earth, and the longest lasted 65 minutes. On Flight 14, Ship is meant to reach orbit, release 26 Starlink satellites, circle Earth six times, and splash down off Chile about 10 hours after launch.

cards.title: Quiet repression in East Germany, still felt decades later
cards.body: Former East Germans who were watched, questioned or harassed by the state report more depression, anxiety and trauma symptoms today, decades later. Their blood also tended to show more of one sign of inflammation. It is one study, so it shows a link, not a cause.
cards.evidence: single study · n=100 (49 repressed, 51 not) · questionnaires + blood markers · no before-measure

sections.text:
A young member of a church group in East Germany is told to come in for questioning. Nobody hits them. Nobody locks them up. They go home the same day. But at work, they are quietly held back. And they start to wonder which friend is reporting on them.

East Germany (the German Democratic Republic, or GDR) was a one-party state from 1949 until 1990. It used quiet tools like these against people it saw as trouble: artists, church groups, youth subcultures, people who wanted to leave. Researchers call this "soft repression". It means being watched, being questioned, denunciation (being secretly reported by others) and harassment at school or work. It is not torture or prison. Often it does not even count as trauma in the usual sense. A new study asks if it still leaves a mark decades later, in both mind and body.

The idea is simple. Soft repression does not hurt once and stop. It creates a feeling that never quite switches off: insecurity, mistrust, and the need to watch everything you say and do. That is long-term stress. Long-term stress has been linked to anxiety, depression, a stress system that stops working properly, and changes in the immune system. This is how fear can get "under the skin".

Ruth Marheinecke and her colleagues found 100 former GDR citizens, aged 50 to 78, mostly from Thuringia and Saxony. Forty-nine had faced at least two of these methods. Fifty-one had lived in the GDR with no personal experience of repression. The two groups were alike in age, gender and region. Everyone filled in questionnaires on depression, anxiety, trauma symptoms, resilience (the ability to bounce back) and support from other people. Everyone also gave blood.

The blood tests looked at three things. Interleukin-6 is a signal the immune system uses; more of it means more inflammation in the body. hs-CRP is another, very sensitive sign of inflammation. Telomeres are protective caps on the ends of our chromosomes; shorter caps suggest cells are aging faster.

The results were mixed, and that matters. The repression group scored higher on depression, anxiety and trauma symptoms, and lower on resilience. Their interleukin-6 tended to be higher. But hs-CRP and telomere length were the same in both groups.

One detail stood out. Inside the repression group, people with less support from others had shorter telomeres. The authors say support may help protect cells from aging. That is a possibility, not a proven fact.

The authors are honest about the limits. Nobody measured these people before the repression, and this was not an experiment. So we cannot know if the repression caused the differences, or if something else did. One detail points the other way. People with serious mental illness today were not allowed to take part. So the study may include mostly the tougher survivors, and the real effect could be bigger.

For the church-group member, the questioning ended long ago. This study suggests that, for many like them, the mind and possibly the blood still remember it.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: One small study of 100 people, found through flyers, newspaper ads and church communities. It shows a link, not a cause. Only one of three blood markers, interleukin-6, tended to differ.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Repression does not need prison bars. The constant fear of being watched may stay with a person for decades.

recall.q: What did the study find in former East Germans who faced soft repression, and why can't it say the repression caused it?
recall.a: They reported more depression, anxiety and trauma symptoms, and lower resilience. Their interleukin-6, a sign of inflammation, also tended to be higher. But no one measured them before the repression, and it was not an experiment, so something else could explain the difference.

cards.title: Does quantum physics describe reality, or our part in it?
cards.body: Quantum physics predicts with amazing accuracy, yet it cannot say what one single particle will do. For a century, physicists have argued about where that gap lives: in nature, or in us. Philosopher Michel Bitbol gives a third answer. The gap exists because we are part of the world we measure.

sections.text:
In October 1927, the people who built quantum mechanics met in Brussels, at the Solvay Conference. They could not agree on who does the choosing. When a tiny particle did something no one could predict, some spoke of a "choice of the observer." Others spoke of a "choice of nature."

The puzzle comes from three limits in the theory. First, you cannot predict a single event at the smallest scale. You can only give odds. Second, some pairs of properties, like where a particle is and how it is moving, cannot both be known exactly at the same time. This is Heisenberg's famous principle. Third, some physicists propose a basic rule: there is a limit to how much useful information you can ever get from a physical system.

These limits do not weaken the theory. They drive its success. Because of Heisenberg's principle, nothing can have exactly zero energy. So even empty space pushes on two metal plates set very close together. This is the Casimir effect, and it can be measured.

So the fight is not about whether the theory works. It is about what it describes. Heisenberg himself went back and forth. He used three German words for his principle, meaning uncertainty, imprecision, and indeterminacy. The first two point to a gap in what we know about a world that is fixed underneath. The third suggests that nature itself is not fixed.

Most physicists answer in one of two ways. Either the theory is incomplete, and the chance is a hole in our picture. Or the theory is complete, and nature really is random. The two camps disagree, but they share one belief. The theory describes the world as it is on its own, apart from us.

Michel Bitbol is a philosopher and a former research director at CNRS, France's national research centre. He says both camps make the same hidden mistake. They split knowing into two boxes: the subject (the one who observes) and the object (the world being observed). Then they ask which box holds the chance. Bitbol's answer is different. Probability sits at the core of physics because we act inside our environment. We never just watch from outside, and we cannot be pulled apart from the world. So the odds are not only a flaw in our knowledge. They are not only a feature of a world without us either. They are the mark of our taking part. At its strongest, this view does not pick a side in the 1927 argument. It rejects the choice itself.

Now the realist reply. The physicist Antony Valentini says quantum mechanics is a plain description of material reality, the stuff out there. It is just incomplete. The chance we see is a hole in the theory, not in the world.

Here is the crux. Both sides use the same theory and get the same predictions. So the dispute is about meaning, not measurement. The realist bets that a fuller picture of the world, without us in it, is possible. Bitbol bets that for this theory, that is the wrong question. His essay names no experiment that could decide between them.

A century after Brussels, physicists have not settled it. The realist reading is the more common habit, but habit is not proof. Bitbol's best point is that the choice was never only between two options.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you ask whether chance lives in you or in the world, ask whether you and the world were ever really two.

recall.q: One camp says quantum chance comes from an incomplete theory. The other says nature itself is random. What third option does Bitbol offer?
recall.a: Bitbol says probability is built into physics because we act inside our environment and cannot be separated from the world. So quantum chance is not only a gap in our knowledge, and not only nature's randomness. It is the mark of our taking part in the world we measure.

cards.title: Stanislas Dehaene and the fight over how children learn
cards.body: Stanislas Dehaene has spent forty years mapping how the brain learns to read and count. He expected French schools to follow the evidence. After eight years advising the government, children's scores have barely moved. The evidence ran into teachers' pride, unions and politics.

sections.text:
Autumn light falls from a skylight onto shelves of French law books. In this small library inside France's education ministry, Stanislas Dehaene opens his laptop and gives his colleagues bad news. The newspaper Le Monde has called his council racist, and it will not print his reply. He asks them to share the reply online instead.

Dehaene is a world-famous cognitive neuroscientist (a scientist who studies how the brain produces thought). Since 2018 he has led the Scientific Council for National Education, which advises the French government on how children learn. More than ten years ago, he set out to bring four decades of brain research into schools. He thought the evidence would speak for itself. It did not.

His central idea is also the heart of his reply to Le Monde. Human brains share one basic plan. When his lab scans different people, the same circuits light up for reading and for maths. So when a child fails, Dehaene looks first at the teaching, not the child.

Numbers show this. Even maths students take longer to pick the bigger of 5 and 6 than the bigger of 1 and 9. The brain senses quantity roughly before it learns exact symbols. Children bring this number sense to school, and Dehaene argues that schools waste it. They give out worksheets full of symbols too early. They stop children counting on their fingers. But finger-counting is a bridge to abstract maths, not a crutch.

Reading shows it even more clearly. His team found a brain region that recognises written letters. He calls it the letterbox. In adults who never learned to read, it barely responds to words. What switches it on best is phonics: teaching, step by step, which letters make which sounds. Yet most French schools use mixed methods. These blend phonics with whole language, the false belief that children learn to read naturally by guessing words from their shape and context. One study in poor Paris suburbs found that only 4 per cent of first-grade teachers used step-by-step phonics. 77 per cent used mixed methods. A third of the children read fewer than 30 to 40 words a minute. Dehaene notes that the children who succeed anyway often have families filling the gaps at home.

Then came the backlash. Teachers' unions saw science being used to overrule their professional judgment. When the ministry put out a phonics guide shaped by his council, the unions compared it to Mao's Little Red Book. A respected psychiatrist called his approach eugenics (the old, rejected idea of ranking people by biology). Critics said he placed children's problems in their brains, not in their families or their poverty. Dehaene answered that he is neither left nor right, only a scientist.

Progress has been slow. After eight years, he says, French scores are changing "a tiny little bit". More than one in four children still start secondary school unable to read or do maths with confidence. Looking at poor maths results one day, he said quietly that teachers "want pedagogical freedom, but look at the results."

His story shows why good evidence so rarely reaches the classroom. Research does not land on empty ground. It lands on teachers' sense of who they are, on unions, on politics and on old beliefs about childhood. A brain scan can show a circuit. It cannot make a teacher feel respected. It cannot tell a parent their child is not a test subject. Dehaene now seems to understand this. With the researcher Cassandra Potier Watkins, he started a nonprofit, Excello, that builds classroom materials based on the evidence. He is no longer only telling teachers what works. He is trying to put it in their hands.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The critics are not only defending habit. A kindergarten teacher made their best point plainly: what happens under a microscope ignores whether a child has eaten, slept or feels safe. Dehaene himself opened his book How We Learn with a blind seven-year-old boy who, he wrote, made him rethink his ideas about learning. And the phonics fight is much older than him. California's reading scores fell after it adopted whole language in the late 1980s, long before his brain scans.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: All human brains share the same circuits for reading and numbers. So when a child fails, Dehaene blames the teaching first.
The brain senses rough quantity before exact symbols, so finger-counting helps children. For reading, step-by-step phonics works best.
In one poor Paris area, only 4 per cent of first-grade teachers used step-by-step phonics.
Pushback came from teachers' pride, unions, and a fear that brain science ignores poverty and home life.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Being right is where changing a classroom starts, not where it ends.

recall.q: What is Dehaene's central idea about how children learn, and what does his slow progress in France show about evidence in education?
recall.a: All human brains share the same circuits for reading and numbers. So when children fail, the teaching is usually the problem, for example a lack of step-by-step phonics. But after eight years, scores have barely moved. Teachers' pride, unions, politics and old beliefs pushed back. Evidence alone rarely changes a classroom.

cards.title: Affect theory: when the humanities turned to the body
cards.body: For a long time, many scholars said the self is built mostly out of words. In the mid-1990s, some thinkers pushed back. They looked to the body instead.

sections.text:
What was the old view?

In the humanities (the study of philosophy, literature and culture), a popular idea said language makes up most of who we are. Words, labels, the stories we tell about ourselves: these build the self.

What changed in the mid-1990s?

Some thinkers challenged that view. They did not throw language away. They said it was not the whole story. To explain how people build their worlds, they turned to the body. This shift is called the "affective turn." A "turn" just means a field changing where it looks.

Who led it?

A video essay by the UK video essayist Lewis Waller follows two figures. One is Brian Massumi, a Canadian philosopher. The other is Eve Sedgwick, a US literary critic. Both studied the embodied, meaning what we live through in the body. They also studied the visceral, meaning what we feel in the gut, below words.

What problem were they trying to solve?

An old split in Western philosophy, called the mind-body divide. It treats the mind and the body as two separate things: thoughts in one place, flesh in another. Affect theory tries to bridge that gap. The aim, in the video's words, is to "think about ideas and matter at the same time." Matter here means physical stuff, like the body.

So is affect just emotion?

The short video does not draw a neat line between the two. It places the theory where three things meet: the body, emotion and identity. It is close to a neighbouring idea called embodied cognition. This says we think with the whole body, not only the brain. What the video does make clear is the direction: start from the feeling body, not from the sentence.

What can't it answer yet?

The question it started with. If ideas and matter are really one thing, how do we think about both at once? And how do we stop one from quietly swallowing the other? The affective turn names this bridge as its goal. Whether anyone has fully built it is still an open question.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you have the words, your body has already taken a position.

recall.q: What idea did the 'affective turn' push against, and where did it look instead?
recall.a: It pushed against the view that the self is built mostly through language. Thinkers like Massumi and Sedgwick looked to the body and gut-level feeling instead, hoping to bridge philosophy's old split between mind and body.

cards.title: South Korea summons Ukraine's envoy over two North Korean prisoners
cards.body: South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador, Andrii Vieshkin, to make a formal complaint. Last Wednesday, at the UN General Assembly, President Zelensky announced that Ukraine had handed two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Seoul says this was meant to stay secret. Kyiv says it never agreed to that.

sections.text:
Seoul gives two reasons for the secrecy. First, it wanted to protect the soldiers' families in North Korea. Second, it says Kyiv wanted silence too, so that no one would ask why Ukraine did not swap the men for captured Ukrainians.

Zelensky's office says there was no non-disclosure agreement (a promise to keep something private). Seoul says that is false and wants an apology.

The two men fought for Russia. They were captured in Russia's Kursk region in early 2025. They had told local media they wanted to go to South Korea.

sections.label: The numbers
items: More than 1 year: how long Seoul and Kyiv talked before the handover
$100 million: South Korea's July aid package to Ukraine. It adds to earlier non-lethal help, like helmets, body armour and medical equipment

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The leak hurts President Lee Jae Myung at home. His party is trying to restart peace talks with North Korea. The opposition says he hid the handover to keep the North happy. The fight also adds to an old tension: Kyiv wants South Korean anti-air missiles, but Seoul does not give lethal weapons to countries at war.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Will Ukraine apologise? Will Seoul keep its no-weapons rule? Russia has warned it will hit back if South Korea arms Ukraine. It has not said how.

recall.q: Why did South Korea summon Ukraine's envoy, and what does Kyiv say in reply?
recall.a: Zelensky publicly announced that Ukraine had handed two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. Seoul says the handover was meant to stay secret, partly to protect the soldiers' families, and wants an apology. Kyiv says there was never an agreement to keep it secret.

cards.title: Autism and online extremism: what we know and don't
cards.body: Some research suggests some autistic people may be more drawn to extremist content online. But the evidence is thin. The real danger seems to come from loneliness, bullying and lack of support, not from autism itself.
cards.evidence: research review · little tested evidence · mostly forensic case studies

sections.text:
Some autistic people charged with or convicted of terror-related crimes describe moving from one extremist group to the next. They were not chasing one idea. They were looking for a place to belong.

That detail matters now. Media reports in Australia suggest neo-Nazis may be trying to recruit autistic young men. Neophytos Georgiou, a researcher in this area, explains what the evidence can and cannot say.

First, what we know. Some research, including his own, suggests some autistic people may be more likely to get involved with harmful content online, such as conspiracy theories and extremist ideas. A 2024 study he led found some evidence that certain autistic traits may make people more likely to believe misinformation.

Three traits come up. The first is fixated interests, which means an intense focus on one subject. Usually this is a gift. It leads to friends, study and meaningful work. It becomes a problem only when the subject is harmful. The second is rigid thinking. This makes it harder to weigh arguments against your view. If a recruiter repeats the same message for months, a person's view can narrow and harden. The third is a love of order and routine. Extremist groups sell black-and-white answers and clear rules for how to think. That pulls in neurotypical (non-autistic) people too. But it may feel especially calming to someone who finds the world chaotic.

We also know something about circumstances. Autistic children and young people are much more likely to be bullied, left out and lonely. Many are left feeling unwanted, powerless, and somehow at fault. Extremism offers the opposite story: take back your power, and join a community of people like you.

Now, what we don't know. We don't know how big any added risk is, or how common this path is. Extremist activity is often secret or illegal, so the people involved are nearly impossible to study. Georgiou's review found little tested evidence. The best source so far is forensic case studies: detailed reports on single criminal cases. They show how one person got there. They cannot show how often it happens, or say anything about autistic people in general.

What is still argued over is the cause: traits or situations. Extremism researchers warn that autism alone does not explain why someone engages with this content or turns violent. Georgiou says the traits matter only when combined with being young, isolated and poorly supported. Most autistic people never go near extremism. Looking only at traits misses how recruiters use exclusion and unmet needs.

How would we learn more? Partly by testing support. There is some evidence that specialist support for at-risk autistic young people improves wellbeing, builds stronger relationships and moves them away from radical ideas. But much more work is needed.

For worried parents, the advice is simple. Keep talking. Don't mock, and don't confront.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The trait findings are early and hedged. They show some autistic people may be more open to misinformation. They do not show that autism causes extremism.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Recruiters sell belonging. The best protection is to offer it first.

recall.q: If autism itself is not the problem, what makes some autistic young people vulnerable to extremist recruiters?
recall.a: Their situation. Traits like fixated interests and rigid thinking may add risk only when combined with being young, isolated and poorly supported. Recruiters use bullying, loneliness and exclusion, and offer power and a place to belong. Most autistic people never go near extremism.

cards.title: The orca mother who carried her dead calf for 17 days
cards.body: Maria Popova argues that this mother's grief is not a flaw. It comes from the same deep bonds that make orcas the top hunters of the ocean. Having those bonds means paying for them when someone dies.

sections.text:
A mother orca swims with her dead calf resting on her head. It is 2018, in Puget Sound. For seventeen days she carries it across a thousand miles of ocean. She hardly eats. She can barely keep up with her pod (her family group). People around the world follow her story, and NPR calls it her "tour of grief."

Maria Popova writes The Marginalian. At the time she was living on a small island in those same waters, finishing her first book. In early 2025 the same mother lost another calf. Again she carried it for seventeen days. Loss like this is common for orcas. About two in three orca pregnancies end in miscarriage or in the baby's death.

To see why her grief matters, look at how orcas live. We call them killer whales, but they are really the largest kind of dolphin. They are apex predators, meaning nothing hunts them. They hunt everything from seals to the blue whale, the largest animal on Earth. Their secret is not strength. It is teamwork.

Take a seal resting on sea ice. The pod swims under the ice together and breaks it with a shock wave. They blow bubbles to push the broken pieces apart. Then they turn on their sides and swim as one. This makes a wave big enough to wash over the ice, and the seal falls into the water. The pod then shares the food according to its web of relationships.

The young learn all this by watching. Their teachers are the females, especially old mothers past menopause (the age when they can no longer have babies). Orca families are built around mothers. Sons stay with their mothers for life. One long study called the males "mamma's boys."

Here is the turn. Popova says the hunter and the grieving mother are the same animal, for the same reason. Orcas hunt this well only because they bond this deeply. They depend on each other. Their minds can tell "me" from "you," and still reach across that gap. That same power is what makes a dead calf so hard to put down. You cannot keep the skill and remove the cost.

In people, Popova writes, we call this power love. She points to the philosopher Hannah Arendt, who said loss is the price we pay for love. She adds the poet Rumi, who urged true humans to risk everything for love. Her own answer: love anyway, knowing the bill will come.

So when someone still grieves long after others expect them to move on, it is not weakness. It is not a failure to cope. It shows how much weight the bond was carrying. The mother orca is not broken. She is paying the price of what made her strong.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The bond that makes us strong together is the same bond that makes loss so heavy.

recall.q: Why does Popova say the orca mother's grief and the orcas' skill as hunters come from the same source?
recall.a: Orcas hunt as a team because they bond deeply and their minds reach from self to other. That same closeness makes losing a calf so painful. You cannot have the power of the bond without the cost of losing it. In people, we call this love.

cards.title: Does religious practice really change the brain?
cards.body: A review of 105 brain studies found that prayer, chanting and meditation go with real differences in the brain. Two regions kept showing up: the control center, and the bridge between thinking and feeling. The hard part is proving that the practice caused the differences.
cards.evidence: systematic review · 105 studies · 8 traditions · 1998-2026 · many small, correlational or single-case

sections.text:
From the age of three, a 12th-century nun named Hildegard von Bingen saw shimmering points of light and falling stars. She believed they came from God. Centuries later, the neurologist Oliver Sacks said they were migraine auras. No one can prove either view.

Skeptic: Fine, one nun had visions. But does religious practice actually change the brain? Or do we just find differences in religious people and call them effects?

Expert: A new review gathered 105 studies from 1998 to 2026. They covered eight religious traditions and seven kinds of brain scans. The main finding: these practices go with steady, sometimes lasting changes. Some were in gray matter, the brain tissue packed with nerve cell bodies. Others were in how regions connect. Two areas kept appearing. One is the prefrontal cortex, the brain's control center for planning and managing emotion. The other is the anterior cingulate cortex, which links the thinking areas to the feeling areas.

Skeptic: "Religion" covers a lot. Is it all one effect?

Expert: No. It depends on the practice. Chanting OM calmed the amygdala, the brain's alarm center. Buddhist chanting switched it on instead. Personal prayer in your own words lit up areas used for connecting with other people. A Sahaja yoga prayer, aimed at quiet, forgiveness and humility, worked the other way. It turned down areas for outward attention and top-down control, the brain steering itself on purpose. People who pray Salat daily, an Islamic prayer with set postures, recitation, breathing and focus, showed differences in the corpus callosum, the bridge between the brain's two halves.

Skeptic: What's your strongest case?

Expert: Hindu Vedic priests. They are trained from childhood to memorize thousands of Sanskrit verses. Compared with matched controls, they had a thicker cortex in areas for self-discipline, emotional control, pitch, rhythm and melody. One surprise: the hippocampus, the brain's hub for forming new memories, showed no change.

Skeptic: Here is my real objection. Those priests were chosen as boys. Someone who prays an hour a day for years may have started with a different brain. A scan is a snapshot. It cannot tell you which came first. You can match controls on many things, but not on the pull that drew a person to devotion in the first place.

Expert: That's fair, and the authors partly agree. Many of the studies were small, correlational (they show a link, not a cause) or single case studies. The authors call the results preliminary, a starting point. Even their claim is careful: the differences seem to track how people lived, "if the causal reading holds." Their hope is practical. These practices are already everywhere, free, and accepted in many cultures.

Skeptic: Then what would settle it?

Expert: Following people over time, before and after they take up a practice. But behind that sits a harder question. Take someone with no pull toward faith and give them the same years of chanting. Would their brain change the same way? Or is the devotion itself part of what changes the brain?

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Most people studied were healthy. Only a small group had conditions like depression. So far, religious practice has not been reliably shown to treat diagnosed mental illness.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A brain scan shows where a life has been. It cannot show whether the life shaped the brain, or the brain chose the life.

recall.q: What did the review find about religious practice and the brain, and why can't it yet say the practice caused the differences?
recall.a: Across 105 studies, practices like chanting, prayer and recitation went with consistent brain differences, most often in the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, and the details depended on the practice. But many studies were small, correlational or single cases. People drawn to devotion may have had different brains to begin with, and a snapshot cannot show which came first.

cards.title: How adults feel about their ADHD depends on which kind they have
cards.body: People with ADHD do not all feel the same about their condition. In a new study, adults with more restless, impulsive symptoms saw their ADHD in a more positive way. Adults whose main problem was focus were less likely to see it as a strength.
cards.evidence: three samples · n=84, 125, 126 · self-report · adults only

sections.text:
A leg bounces under a desk and won't stop. In another room, a mind drifts away in the middle of a sentence and comes back five minutes later. Both people can have the same diagnosis: ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder).

ADHD starts in childhood and often lasts into adult life. Doctors look for two groups of symptoms. The first is inattention: trouble focusing, staying on a task, or staying organized. The second is hyperactivity and impulsivity: too much movement, restlessness, acting before thinking. A person can have mostly one group, mostly the other, or both.

For years, research looked mostly at the harm: problems at school, with emotions, in relationships. Then came the neurodiversity movement. Its idea is that brains that work differently are not simply broken. They can have real strengths too. Earlier interview studies found adults with ADHD naming strengths like high energy, unusual thinking, and a hunger for new things.

A team led by Gili Katabi at Tel-Aviv University wanted to measure these good feelings with numbers. They also asked a sharper question: does it matter which kind of ADHD you have?

It does. People with more hyperactive and impulsive symptoms had clearly more positive views of their ADHD. This was true in all three groups studied. People with more inattention leaned the other way. They were less likely to see their ADHD as a strength. But this link was weaker, and not strong enough to be sure of in every group.

Why the difference? The authors suggest one possible reason. Restlessness is easy to see as energy. Spacing out or forgetting things is much harder to call a strength, and society is less kind to it. An older study fits this picture. Young adults with more hyperactivity and impulsivity later said they were more satisfied with their jobs and relationships. Over time, that energy may grow into curiosity and enthusiasm that people learn to value.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: The team built a new questionnaire, the Positive Attitudes Toward ADHD Scale. It covers themes like creativity, energy, and resilience (bouncing back from trouble). People rate each statement from 1 to 5. The team tested it on three groups of adults with ADHD: 84 young adults in Israel, 125 adults in Israel whose diagnosis was checked again by phone interview, and 126 English speakers online from 24 countries. Everyone also reported how often they had each type of symptom over the past six months. In a check with 35 people, the link still held after measuring general life satisfaction. So the scale was measuring feelings about ADHD, not just a happy mood.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: All of this is self-report. It shows how people feel about their ADHD, not whether they really do better. Saying you are creative does not mean you would score higher on a creativity test. The scale also had no questions about hyperfocus: the deep focus on interesting tasks that many people with ADHD describe. Leaving it out may have made inattentive people look less positive than they are. And the study only covered adults, who have had years to accept their condition.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A restless body is easy to call energy. A drifting mind is harder to call a gift, and that shapes how a person sees themselves.

recall.q: Which type of ADHD symptoms went with more positive feelings about the condition, and why might inattentive people feel less positive?
recall.a: More hyperactive and impulsive symptoms went with more positive views of ADHD in all three groups; more inattention leaned toward less positive views. A likely reason: restlessness is easy to see as energy, but spacing out and forgetting are hard to see as strengths, and society is less kind to them.

cards.title: Alzheimer's-type brain damage in mice traced to lymph nodes
cards.body: In mice with Alzheimer's-type disease, the immune cells that damage the brain seem to be prepared in lymph nodes outside the brain. When scientists removed the cells that do this preparing, most of the brain damage went away. The tau tangles did not.
cards.evidence: single study · mice · sample size not stated

sections.text:
Lymph nodes are small lumps that filter fluid for the immune system. Some sit in your neck, far from the parts of the brain that Alzheimer's attacks. Yet a new mouse study suggests they may help decide whether those parts get damaged.

Alzheimer's and related diseases called primary tauopathies share one sign: twisted clumps of a protein called tau in the brain. These brains also hold unusually many T cells. T cells are immune cells whose normal job is to attack infected or foreign cells. Earlier work from David Holtzman's lab at Washington University in St. Louis showed that removing T cells from the brain prevented much of the damage in mice. So the next question was: where do these T cells come from, and what sends them in?

T cells do not choose their targets alone. Helper immune cells called dendritic cells show them what to attack. The type that matters here, called cDC1, is rare in the brain. The few that are there do not seem to work with the T cells that arrive after tau tangles form. So the T cells were probably being prepared somewhere else.

The team removed these dendritic cells from lymph nodes and other places in mice bred to develop tau tangles. Most of the extra T cells in the brain disappeared, especially a kind called CD8 T cells. Most of the brain damage disappeared too, and the mice kept their thinking abilities. But the amount of tau tangles did not change at all.

That is the surprise. The tangles were still there, but without the immune attack they did far less harm. So the body's reaction to tau may be a major cause of the damage, not only tau itself.

How could this work? Holtzman offers an idea that has not been tested yet. Damage from tau may release material from brain cells. That material may travel to the lymph nodes in the neck, where dendritic cells mark it as a target. T cells trained on that target may then travel to the brain.

This matters for treatment. Brain drugs usually have to cross the blood-brain barrier, a tight wall that keeps most substances out of the brain. If the trouble starts outside the brain, a drug may not need to get in. And many ways of controlling T cells are already approved for other diseases.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This was done in mice, not people. The dendritic cells were blocked from birth, which no treatment could do. The team is now testing whether blocking them in midlife, around when tau tangles begin, protects the brain in the same way. They also have not yet found the signal that sends T cells toward the brain.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The tangles stayed and the damage did not. Much of the harm came from how the body reacted to them.

recall.q: What happened when the researchers removed dendritic cells in mice with tau disease, and why was the result surprising?
recall.a: Most of the extra T cells left the brain, brain damage dropped sharply, and the mice kept their thinking abilities. The surprise was that the tau tangles did not change. This suggests much of the damage comes from an immune attack prepared in lymph nodes outside the brain.

cards.title: Frogs under ice: the brain makes its own backup fuel
cards.body: When a bullfrog's sugar runs out after a winter under the ice, its brain makes its own backup fuel. Textbooks say this fuel comes almost entirely from the liver. The finding hints that the brain's need for sugar may be flexible, not fixed.
cards.evidence: single study · animal study (bullfrogs) · sample size not stated

sections.text:
Under the ice of a frozen pond, a bullfrog waits out the winter. Its body has slowed almost to a stop. By late winter the water holds very little oxygen, and the frog's sugar reserves are nearly gone. Then the ice melts. Its brain must switch back on at once to restart breathing and movement.

For a human brain, that would be a disaster. Our brains run on glucose, a sugar carried in the blood. If that supply fails, as it does in a stroke, brain cells stop working quickly. They can die within minutes.

The body does have a backup fuel. When glucose runs low (in starvation, on a keto diet, or during long exercise), the body breaks down fat into small fuel molecules called ketone bodies. The textbook story is that the liver makes them and sends them through the blood to the brain.

A team at the University of Missouri, led by biologist Joseph Santin, found that the bullfrog brain does not wait for the liver. It makes its own ketones, right where they are needed. Santin compares it to finding a backup generator inside a building that everyone thought had only one power source.

Here is how it works. After hibernation (the long winter sleep), the frog's brain circuits can stop using glucose, partly by switching to these home-made ketones. Astrocytes, the support cells that sit beside neurons, make the ketones and pass them to the neurons. The neurons use them to power their synapses, the junctions where one nerve cell signals the next. Genes that break down fat and move ketones around also become more active. And when oxygen was low (a state called hypoxia), the brain-made ketones stopped the usual drop in brain activity.

So a frog can wake in a pond short of both oxygen and sugar and still get its breathing circuits running. It does not have to wait for its slow, cold organs to recover first.

The bigger idea is about brains in general. The authors argue that vertebrates (animals with a backbone) may not be hard-wired to need glucose. That need may be a flexible trait. In some cases, the brain may drop it completely.

This matters for the human mind too. Alzheimer's, ALS, stroke, and schizophrenia all show early problems with how the brain uses glucose. This leaves neurons short of energy. The basic energy machinery of cells is shared across vertebrates. So if scientists learn what switches on the frog's backup, they might one day design drugs that wake a similar system in people.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study, and it was done in frogs. It does not show that human brains can make their own ketones this way. The frog's emergency mode is also temporary, not permanent. Key questions are still open, such as what triggers the switch. Human drugs are a hope for the future, not a result.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain's hunger for sugar may be a setting it can change, not a law it must obey.

recall.q: What did the Missouri team find about where the bullfrog brain gets its backup fuel, and why does that challenge the textbook view?
recall.a: When glucose runs out after hibernation, the frog's brain makes its own ketones: astrocytes produce them and pass them to neurons. Textbooks say ketones come almost entirely from the liver. The finding suggests the brain's need for glucose may be flexible, not hard-wired.

cards.title: Chronic insomnia linked to higher stroke and dementia risk
cards.body: A large review of past research found that people with chronic insomnia had a 26% higher risk of stroke. They were also 28% more likely to end up in hospital. Insomnia also went along with dementia, depression and suicidal behavior. The authors say years of bad sleep may be an early warning sign, not just a nuisance.
cards.evidence: umbrella review · 16 published meta-analyses + 3 new reviews · stroke: 9 studies, 1,343,164 people · observational, not

sections.text:
The clock says 3:12. You have been awake since 1:40. Tomorrow you will feel slow and foggy, and most people would stop the story there. A new review asks a bigger question: what else might those nights be telling us?

The work was led by the European Academy of Neurology and the Medical University of Vienna. It was published in Sleep Medicine Reviews. It is an umbrella review, which means the team ran no new experiment. Instead, they gathered meta-analyses (studies that pool many earlier studies) and read them side by side. They searched up to August 2025 and found 16.

They asked whether insomnia predicts seven things: stroke, dementia, depression, suicide, death, accidents at work, and hospital stays. For three of these, nobody had pooled the data before, so the team did it themselves.

First, stroke. Across nine studies with more than 1.3 million people, those with insomnia had a 26% higher risk. Next, hospital stays. Across five studies with about 518,000 people, those with chronic insomnia were 28% more likely to be admitted to hospital, for any reason.

The older meta-analyses told a steady story. Insomnia kept showing up as a sign of later dementia, especially Alzheimer's disease. It also went with depression and suicidal behavior. But how strong and steady the numbers were changed from one outcome to another.

Two results broke the pattern. Insomnia was not linked to a higher risk of death. And for accidents at work, the team found only two studies, too few to combine. There were hints of a link to fatal accidents and to accidents on the way to work, but the authors say the data are too thin to judge.

What do they want? Stefan Seidel, a sleep specialist in Vienna who started the project, says sleep should be part of every talk about brain health, at every age. He wants insomnia and its treatment taken seriously in schools, workplaces and community health programs. The main point is simple: chronic insomnia is not a small complaint to ignore. It may be an early red flag that the body and brain are starting to struggle.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: These are observational links. They show that insomnia and these illnesses go together, not that one causes the other. The original studies also defined insomnia in different ways. And other things may shape the numbers, such as sleeping pills, or a person's heart and metabolic health before the study began.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A bad night is a tired morning; years of bad nights may be a message worth hearing.

recall.q: What did this umbrella review find about insomnia, stroke and hospital stays, and why can't it say insomnia causes them?
recall.a: Insomnia went with a 26% higher stroke risk (nine studies, over 1.3 million people) and a 28% higher chance of hospital admission (five studies, about 518,000 people). But the data are observational, the studies defined insomnia differently, and things like sleeping pills or heart health could explain part of the link. So insomnia is a warning sign, not a proven cause.

cards.title: Indians pour money into government savings schemes
cards.body: From April to July 2026, the first four months of the 2026-27 financial year, net money coming into India's small savings schemes rose 56% from a year earlier. This is happening even as more ordinary people buy shares.

sections.text:
Small savings schemes are savings plans backed by the government. The "net" figure is new money put in, minus money taken out.

At this pace, collections will cross the government's target of Rs 3.6 lakh crore for the full year. That helps the government meet its budget goals.

The main reason is simple. The interest rates on these schemes are still attractive. More small investors now buy shares, but many still want steady, safe returns.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 56%: rise in net collections, April to July, compared with the same months last year
Rs 3.6 lakh crore: the full-year target, now likely to be beaten

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The stock-market boom has not pulled savers away from safe government schemes. For many people, a sure return still beats a chance at bigger gains.

recall.q: What happened to net money flowing into small savings schemes early in 2026-27, and why?
recall.a: From April to July it rose 56% from a year earlier, so it is on track to beat the Rs 3.6 lakh crore target. Good interest rates keep drawing savers who want steady returns, even as more people buy shares.
